Marius Stakelborough

Biography

Marius Stakelborough (1923–2020) stands immortalized as the beloved cultural patriarch of Saint Barthélemy, a visionary entrepreneur whose life's work profoundly shaped the social fabric of Gustavia. Born into an era when Saint Barthélemy was a remote, impoverished commune of the French West Indies, Stakelborough rose above severe economic adversity to become the island's most unifying figure. As the founder of the historic bar Le Select in 1949, he created far more than a commercial establishment; he established an egalitarian sanctuary where local fishermen, visiting sailors, international expatriates, and wealthy travelers converged on equal footing. Operating simultaneously as a cultural archivist and an unofficial consular representative for Sweden, Stakelborough dedicated over seven decades to preserving the distinct dual heritage of St. Barts. His relentless advocacy bridged the island's colonial Swedish past with its modern French identity, earning him prestigious royal honors and cementing his reputation as the soul of Gustavia.

Early Life in Austerity and Maritime Labor

Marius Stakelborough was born on June 5, 1923, in the harbor town of Gustavia, during a period characterized by profound economic stagnation across Saint Barthélemy. Following the French purchase of the island back from Sweden in 1878, the bustling trade that had once characterized Gustavia's free port had dwindled significantly. When Stakelborough was merely five years old, his mother migrated to Guadeloupe in search of employment, leaving Marius and his brother Philibert to be raised by their grandmother in austere conditions. Formal education on the island was rudimentary and limited; Marius attended the local school from the age of seven until thirteen, developing a voracious appetite for reading and self-education despite the scarcity of books and resources.

Upon completing his primary schooling, young Marius traveled to Guadeloupe to join his mother, gaining early exposure to the broader Caribbean world before returning to his native island. In his late teens and early twenties, he undertook a grueling series of occupations to survive. He worked briefly as a bookseller, a weather station attendant, and a local photographer, capturing rare early snapshots of island life. Most formatively, Stakelborough spent a decade laboring as a merchant mariner and sailor. Navigating schooners and sloops across the treacherous waters separating Saint Barthélemy, Saint Martin, Guadeloupe, and Martinique, he transported essential cargo, livestock, and charcoal. This maritime labor not only instilled in him an enduring respect for seafaring traditions but also forged deep camaraderie with the working-class seamen who would later become the foundational clientele of his historic enterprise.

The Founding of Le Select (1949) and Social Transformation

In November 1949, seeking a more stable livelihood onshore, Marius Stakelborough made a decision that would permanently alter the social landscape of Gustavia. Utilizing his modest savings, he rented a small wooden structure in the heart of the port town and opened a bar and gathering place named Le Select. Named in homage to the classic literary and cultural cafes of Paris, Le Select was conceived as an unpretentious haven dedicated to literature, music, good conversation, and community solidarity. At the time of its opening, Gustavia lacked modern infrastructure; electricity and running water were virtually non-existent, and the bar operated by the warm glow of oil lamps, serving rum and cold beverages cooled by blocks of ice imported via boat.

"Le Select was never merely about commerce; it was founded as an egalitarian institution where the humblest fisherman and the visiting dignitary shared the same table, the same rum, and the same respect."

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, as aviation pioneer Rémy de Haenen began introducing the first adventurous visitors to the island via his daring airplane landings at St. Jean, Le Select served as the primary social nexus where locals and newcomers intersected. Marius cultivated an atmosphere of absolute equality under the shading canopy of the bar's famous mahogany tree. He famously instituted an unwritten code of unpretentiousness: regardless of wealth, social standing, or origin, every patron was treated with identical warmth and hospitality. This commitment turned Le Select into the informal town hall of Gustavia, a place where municipal issues were debated, news was disseminated, and communal bonds were continually forged.

Bridging Worlds: Swedish Heritage and French Identity

Perhaps Stakelborough's most enduring intellectual and cultural contribution was his passionate preservation of Saint Barthélemy's Swedish heritage. For nearly a century (1784–1878), the island had been a Swedish royal colony, named after King Gustav III. While French language and administration returned in the late nineteenth century, remnants of Swedish urban planning, architecture, and family genealogies persisted. Marius recognized that this unique dual identity was St. Barts' greatest cultural asset. He transformed the interior walls of Le Select into a living museum, adorning them with historical maps, portraits of Swedish monarchs, colonial land registries, and yellowed maritime documents.

In his capacity as a community leader, Marius co-founded the Association Saint-Barth des Amis de la Suède (ASBAS), dedicating himself to fostering robust diplomatic, cultural, and genealogical exchanges between Gustavia and Sweden. When Swedish tourists, researchers, or dignitaries arrived at the port, Marius welcomed them with open arms, serving as an unofficial guide and historian. His efforts ensured that the historical memory of the Swedish era was not erased by modernization or assimilation into the broader French departmental system. Instead, he celebrated the synthesis of Swedish civic structure and French Caribbean culture, creating a unique insular pride that resonated across generations.

Unofficial Diplomacy and Royal Recognition

Over the decades, Stakelborough's tireless dedication to Swedish-Saint Barthélemy relations earned him the affectionate and universally respected title of "The Consul of Sweden". Though he never held a formal diplomatic portfolio from the Swedish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, his practical role exceeded that of many official emissaries. He assisted Swedish citizens in distress, facilitated municipal twinning initiatives, and hosted official delegations representing the Swedish Crown.

His profound contributions received formal international validation in 1981 when His Majesty King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden conferred upon Marius Stakelborough the prestigious Order of the Northern Star (Nordstjärneorden). This knighthood acknowledged his exceptional service in preserving Swedish heritage abroad. Decades later, in August 2011, Marius traveled to Sweden to receive the civic medal of Piteå, the Swedish sister city of Gustavia, further solidifying the permanent fraternal bond he had single-handedly revitalized. Alongside political figures such as Georges Lédée, Marius worked harmoniously to ensure that local municipal policies respected historic architectural norms and heritage sites dating back to the Swedish free-port regime.

The Jimmy Buffett Connection and International Fame

While Le Select was already a revered local institution, it achieved legendary global status through Marius's enduring friendship with American singer-songwriter Jimmy Buffett. Visiting Saint Barthélemy in the early 1970s, Buffett was captivated by the laid-back, welcoming ethos of Le Select and formed an immediate, lifelong kinship with Marius. The bar became Buffett's island sanctuary and creative refuge; he frequently referred to his favorite table beneath the courtyard tree as his "office."

"Marius taught us all how to live with grace, humor, and simplicity. He made a small corner of the Caribbean feel like home to the entire world." — Jimmy Buffett

Buffett's iconic 1978 hit song "Cheeseburger in Paradise" was heavily inspired by the ambiance and culinary simplicity of Le Select, immortalizing the venue in popular culture. Despite international fame and an influx of celebrities, Marius steadfastly refused to gentrify or commercialize the establishment. He maintained affordable prices, retained plastic chairs and simple wooden tables, and continued serving the beloved "Marius Special" burger. To celebrate the bar's 50th, 60th, and 70th anniversaries, Buffett performed free, impromptu concerts in the streets of Gustavia, drawing thousands of revelers who gathered to honor Marius and his philosophy of joyful, unpretentious living.

Patriarch of Gustavia and Enduring Legacy

Marius Stakelborough passed away peacefully on June 18, 2020, at the remarkable age of 97, surrounded by his extensive family and the community he had nurtured for nearly a century. His passing was mourned as the end of an era across the Caribbean and Sweden. Flags across Saint Barthélemy flew at half-mast, and tributes poured in from international diplomats, cultural icons, and ordinary islanders alike.

Today, Le Select remains managed by his children and grandchildren, preserved exactly as Marius intended: a vibrant monument to egalitarianism, historical consciousness, and Caribbean hospitality. Through his extraordinary life, Marius Stakelborough proved that cultural preservation and community solidarity could withstand the pressures of rapid modernization and luxury tourism. He remains eternally enshrined as the gentle patriarch of Gustavia, whose wisdom and warmth bridged oceans, generations, and cultures.

Major Contributions

  • Marius Stakelborough made profound contributions to the cultural preservation, social cohesion, and historical identity of Saint Barthélemy.
  • By founding Le Select in 1949, he established an enduring egalitarian community institution that served as the social and civic heart of Gustavia for over seventy years, resisting commercial gentrification and providing a gathering place where locals, mariners, and visitors interacted on equal terms.
  • Furthermore, Stakelborough acted as the primary architect of modern cultural diplomacy between Saint Barthélemy and the Kingdom of Sweden.
  • Through his tireless archival preservation, his co-founding of the Association Saint-Barth des Amis de la Suède, and his decades of service as unofficial consular representative, he successfully revitalized awareness of the island's Swedish colonial heritage.
  • His exemplary efforts were recognized internationally when he was knighted with the Swedish Order of the Northern Star in 1981, leaving a permanent legacy of cross-cultural unity and insular pride.
